Emmett Till was robbed of his life but also of his own unique Black future. And to remember him is to honor not only the life stolen from him, but the one he deserved to live.

This weekend, I visited "If Emmett Till Lived," the powerful new exhibition in Chicago that affirms the fullness of the man he could have become.

I was honored to select a work of art and contribute a reflection for this exhibit, and it was a joy to spend time with the visionary @sarahelizalewis and Rev. Wheeler Parker Jr., Emmett's cousin, best friend, and last surviving witness to his kidnapping, who helped bring it to life.

For the first time, I invoked Emmett Till's name and didn't feel heaviness. Instead, I was immersed in blissful opportunities to imagine him as a father, a husband, and a Black man who loved softball and dreamed of being a police officer.

While the strange fruit of Black bodies hang from trees across America and Black history is under attack, exhibitions like these are a necessary reminder not only of America's legacy of lynching and racial terror—but also of the Black futures that are lost when Black lives are stolen.

It's why I'll continue demanding a thorough, transparent, and comprehensive federal investigation into the suspicious deaths of Black folks found hanging across the country, as authorized by the Emmett Till Antilynching Act of 2022.

It's why I'll continue defending Black history and our museums—including the Smithsonian and other cultural institutions—from the unprecedented, anti-Black, and fascist assault from the occupant of the White House.

And it's why I'll always fight for Black lives, Black families, Black futures, and our collective liberation.

"If Emmett Till Lived" will be on display until December 19th and you can check it out at the Museum of Contemporary Photography on S Michigan Ave in Chicago.
